## Today's plan

In this lecture, we will look at three questions:

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
## Does adding predictors improve a regression
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
## Is a linear model an adequate description of the relationship?
:::

<br>

::: {.callout-note}
## What does an individual predictor contribute after accounting for the other predictors?
:::

# Comparing regression models {background-color="#40666e"}

## Comparing regression models {style="font-size: 65%;"}

### Why compare models

Suppose we are interested in explaining a response variable $Y$.


:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Model A {.center}

$$
\text{Model A:}\qquad E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1
$$

:::
::: {.column}

### Model B {.center}

$$
\text{Model B:}\qquad E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\beta_3X_3
$$


:::
::::

Model B includes all the terms in Model A, plus two additional predictors.

::: {.callout-note}
## Model A is the reduced model
:::
::: {.callout-note}
## Model B is the full model
:::
::: {.callout-note}
## Model A is nested within Model B
:::

<br>

[**Do the two additional predictors improve the model enough to justify including them?**]{.center}

## What happens when we add predictors?

Adding predictors cannot increase the residual sum of squares (SSE).

$$
\operatorname{SSE}(B)\leq \operatorname{SSE}(A)
$$

- The full model will always fit the observed data at least as well as
the reduced model.
- However, a smaller SSE does not automatically mean that the larger model is
  better. The reduction could simply be due to fitting random variation in the
  sample.
- We need to assess whether the reduction in SSE is large relative to the
  remaining residual variation.

## Comparing the variation explained by two models {style="font-size: 80%;"}

For a regression model containing an intercept,

$$
\operatorname{SST}=\operatorname{SSR}+\operatorname{SSE}
$$

For the two models:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SST}
&=\operatorname{SSR}(A)+\operatorname{SSE}(A)\\
\operatorname{SST}
&=\operatorname{SSR}(B)+\operatorname{SSE}(B)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total sum of squares is the same,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{SSE}(A)-\operatorname{SSE}(B)
=
\operatorname{SSR}(B)-\operatorname{SSR}(A)
}
$$

So, the reduction in SSE is exactly the additional variation explained by
the full model.

## The partial $F$-test {style="font-size: 80%;"}

Consider two nested models:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Reduced model A:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\cdots+\beta_qX_q,\\
\text{Full model B:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\cdots+\beta_kX_k,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $q<k$.

The full model adds $k-q$ predictors.


::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We test:

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0:\quad &\beta_{q+1}=\cdots=\beta_k=0,\\
H_A:\quad &\text{at least one added coefficient is non-zero.}
\end{aligned}
$$

In words:

- $H_0$: the additional predictors do not improve the model.
- $H_A$: at least one additional predictor contributes to the model.

:::

## The partial $F$-statistic {style="font-size: 65%;"}

The test statistic compares the reduction in SSE with the residual variation
remaining in the full model:

$$
\boxed{
F= \frac{
  \{\operatorname{SSE}(A)-\operatorname{SSE}(B)\}/(k-q)}
  {\operatorname{SSE}(B)/(n-k-1)}
}
$$

Under $H_0$,

$$
F\sim F_{k-q,\,n-k-1}
$$

Here:

- $n$ is the number of observations.
- $k-q$ is the number of additional predictors.
- $n-k-1$ is the residual degrees of freedom in the full model.


::: {.callout-tip}
## We reject $H_0$ when the observed $F$-statistic is sufficiently large.
:::

::: {.callout-tip appearance="minimal"}
A large $F$-statistic indicates that the reduction in SSE is large relative
to the residual variation in the full model.
:::

## When can we use this test? {style="font-size: 90%;"}

The partial $F$-test is appropriate when:

- The models are **nested**: every term in the reduced model also appears in the full model.
- Both models are fitted to the same response and the same observations.
- The usual assumptions of the normal linear model are appropriate for the test.

The test can compare models that differ by one or several terms.

For example, we can test whether two predictors should be added together, or whether one predictor should be removed from a larger model.

## Let's do an example

### The steam data

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-1a
tribble(
  ~Variable , ~Description                        ,
  "Steam"   , "Pounds of steam used per month"    ,
  "Temp"    , "Average atmospheric temperature"   ,
  "Inv"     , "Fatty acid inventory"              ,
  "Prod"    , "Pounds of crude glycerin produced" ,
  "Wind"    , "Average wind velocity"             ,
  "Cday"    , "Calendar days in the month"        ,
  "Opday"   , "Operating days in the month"       ,
  "Fday"    , "Days below 32°F"                   ,
  "Wind2"   , "Average wind velocity squared"     ,
  "Start"   , "Number of production start-ups"
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

## Let's do an example

### The steam data

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-1b
tribble(
  ~Variable , ~Description                        ,
  "Steam"   , "Pounds of steam used per month"    ,
  "Temp"    , "Average atmospheric temperature"   ,
  "Inv"     , "Fatty acid inventory"              ,
  "Prod"    , "Pounds of crude glycerin produced" ,
  "Wind"    , "Average wind velocity"             ,
  "Cday"    , "Calendar days in the month"        ,
  "Opday"   , "Operating days in the month"       ,
  "Fday"    , "Days below 32°F"                   ,
  "Wind2"   , "Average wind velocity squared"     ,
  "Start"   , "Number of production start-ups"
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE) |>
  style_tt(i = 2:4, background = "skyblue")
```

## Let's do an example

### Comparing two models

We will compare:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Model A:}\quad
&E(\text{Steam})=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{Temp}\\
\text{Model B:}\quad
&E(\text{Steam})=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{Temp}
+\beta_2\text{Inv}+\beta_3\text{Prod}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Model B adds `Inv` and `Prod` to the model containing `Temp`.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-2
#| echo: true
model_A <- lm(steam ~ temp, data = steam)
model_B <- lm(steam ~ temp + inv + prod, data = steam)
```

## Let's do an example

### Comparing two models

```{r}
#| label: chunk-3a
#| echo: true

summary(model_A)
```

## Let's do an example

### Comparing two models

```{r}
#| label: chunk-3b
#| echo: true

summary(model_B)
```

## Let's do an example {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Comparing two models in R

We can compare the two nested models directly using `anova()`

```{r}
#| label: chunk-4a
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

anova(model_A, model_B)
```

This performs the partial $F$-test.

<br>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

### Null hypothesis {.center}

$$
H_0:\quad \beta_2=\beta_3=0
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Alternative hypothesis {.center}

$$
H_A:\quad \text{at least one of }\; \beta_2,\beta_3\ne 0.
$$


:::
::::

::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}
The test asks whether `inv` and `prod`, considered together,
improve the model after accounting for `temp`.
:::

## Calculating the $F$-statistic by hand {style="font-size: 60%;"}

For these models:

- $n=25$ observations.
- Model A has 2 parameters: an intercept and `temp`.
- Model B has 4 parameters: an intercept and three predictors.
- The full model therefore has $25 - 4 = 21$ residual degrees of freedom.
- Two predictors are added

The residual sums of squares are:

$$
\operatorname{SSE}(A)=18.223, \qquad \operatorname{SSE}(B)=8.927.
$$

Therefore,

$$
F_{\text{obs}} = \frac{(18.223-8.927)/2}{8.927/21} = 10.93
$$

Under the null hypothesis: $F\sim F_{2,21}$. As such, the p-value is
less than 0.01

We reject $H_0$: there is evidence that adding `inv` and `prod` improves the
model.

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-4b
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

anova(model_A, model_B)
```


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important appearance="minimal"}

The partial $F$-test does not ask whether the full model has a smaller SSE.
It must have a smaller or equal SSE.

Instead, it asks:

[Is the reduction in SSE large enough to justify the additional parameters?]{.alert}

:::
::::

# Sequential sum of squares {background-color="#40666e"}

## Sequential sums of squares {style="font-size: 80%;"}

### Adding predictors one at a time

We can also build a regression model by adding predictors sequentially.

For the steam data, consider:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Model A:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0,\\
\text{Model B:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1,\\
\text{Model C:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2,\\
\text{Model D:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1X_1+\beta_2X_2+\beta_3X_3.
\end{aligned}
$$

where:

- $X_1=\text{temp}$
- $X_2=\text{inv}$
- $X_3=\text{prod}$

## What does each predictor add? {style="font-size: 80%;"}

The additional variation explained when moving from Model A to Model B is:

$$
\operatorname{SSR}(B\mid A) = \operatorname{SSR}(B)-\operatorname{SSR}(A)
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{SSR}(C\mid B) &=\operatorname{SSR}(C)-\operatorname{SSR}(B)\\
\operatorname{SSR}(D\mid C) &=\operatorname{SSR}(D)-\operatorname{SSR}(C)
\end{aligned}
$$

These are called **sequential sums of squares**

Each value measures the additional variation explained by a predictor when
it is added to the predictors already in the model.

## Sequential sums of squares for the steam data

<br>

```{r}
tribble(
  ~`Predictor added` , ~`Additional df` , ~`Sequential SS` ,
  "temp"             ,                1 , 45.592           ,
  "inv"              ,                1 ,  9.292           ,
  "prod"             ,                1 ,  0.004           ,
) |>
  tt() |>
  style_tt(i = 0, bold = TRUE)
```

The total regression sum of squares for the full model is approximately:

$$
\operatorname{SSR}(D) = 45.592+9.292+0.004 = 54.888
$$


::: {.callout-important}
## `prod` explains very little additional variation after `temp` and `inv` have already been included
:::

## Obtaining sequential sums of squares in R

The `anova()` function applied to a single `lm` model reports sequential
sums of squares

```{r}
#| label: chunk-5
#| echo: true
model_B <- lm(steam ~ temp + inv + prod, data = steam)

anova(model_B)
```

## Obtaining sequential sums of squares in R {style="font-size: 90%;"}

### The order matters

- Suppose `temp` and `inv` are related to one another.
- If `temp` enters the model first, it receives credit for the variation it explains,
  including variation that it shares with `inv`.
- When `inv` enters second, it is only credited with the additional variation it explains
  after `temp` has been included.
- If we reverse the order, the allocation of shared variation changes.

::: {.callout-important}
## Sequential sums of squares depend on the order in which predictors enter the model
:::

## Testing sequential sums of squares

Each sequential sum of squares can be tested using a partial $F$-test.

For example, to test whether `prod` contributes after `temp` and `inv`, compare:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Reduced model C:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{temp}+\beta_2\text{inv},\\
\text{Full model D:}\quad
&E(Y)=\beta_0+\beta_1\text{temp}
+\beta_2\text{inv}+\beta_3\text{prod}
\end{aligned}
$$

## Sequential and adjusted sums of squares {style="font-size: 80%;"}

There are [different ways]{.alert} to allocate explained variation among predictors.

- **Type I sums of squares:** sequential (depend on the order of predictors).
- **Type II sums of squares:** assess each predictor after accounting for the
  other main effects.

For example, the `car` package provides Type II sums of squares:

```{r}
#| label: chunk-6
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
car::Anova(model_B, type = 2)
```

# Testing for lack of fit {background-color="#40666e"}

## Why check for lack of fit?

A regression model can have statistically significant coefficients and
still be an inadequate description of the relationship.

For example, a straight line may not describe a curved relationship very well.

We therefore need to distinguish between:

- **A predictor having a relationship with the response.**
- **The chosen regression model adequately describing that relationship.**

A formal lack-of-fit test can help assess whether a specified regression
model is appropriate.

## When can we test for lack of fit?

A formal lack-of-fit test requires **replicated observations**.

This means that we have multiple response observations at one or more identical combinations of predictor values.

For simple linear regression, we need repeated observations at the same
values of $X$.

These replicates allow us to estimate the random variation in the response
without relying on the fitted regression line.

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-7
replicated_data <- tibble(
  x = rep(1:5, each = 5),
  y = rep(1:5, each = 5) + rnorm(25, 0, 0.5)
)

replicated_data |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Predictor",
    y = "Response"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Some notation

Suppose we have:

- $g$ distinct values of the predictor, $X$.
- $n_i$ observations at the $i^{\text{th}}$ value of $X$.
- $n=\sum_{i=1}^{g}n_i$ observations in total.

Let $y_{ij}$ denote the $j$th response observed at the $i$th predictor value.

The average response at the $i$th predictor value is:

$$
\bar y_{i} = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}y_{ij}
$$

## Two ways to describe the data

We can fit two different models

<br>

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

### Simple linear regression {.center}

$$
Y_{ij}=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_{ij}
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Means model {.center}

$$
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\varepsilon_{ij}
$$

:::
::::

- Model 1: assumes that the expected response follows a straight line
- Model 2: gives each distinct value of $X$ its own expected response
  - it does not require the group means to lie on a straight line

## Pure error {style="font-size: 60%;"}

The means model allows us to measure the variation among observations that
share the same value of $X$.

The **pure error sum of squares** is:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{SS}_{PE} = \sum_{i=1}^{g}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i} (y_{ij}-\bar y_{i})^2
}
$$

This measures the variation of individual observations around their group means.

Its degrees of freedom are:

$$
df_{PE} = \sum_{i=1}^{g}(n_i-1) = n-g
$$

The pure error mean square is:

$$
\operatorname{MS}_{PE} = \frac{\operatorname{SS}_{PE}}{n-g}
$$

It provides an estimate of the error variance, $\sigma^2$

## Why is pure error useful?

- The pure error estimate is obtained from variation among [observations
  with identical predictor values]{.alert}.
- It [does not depend on]{.alert} whether the regression relationship is linear.
- This gives us a way to [estimate the random variation]{.alert} in the data
  [independently]{.alert} of the fitted regression line.
- In contrast, the residual sum of squares from simple linear regression
  includes both:
  - random variation among replicated observations
  - any systematic lack of fit caused by the straight-line model

## Separating residual variation {style="font-size: 80%;"}

The regression residual sum of squares can be decomposed into:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{SSE} = \operatorname{SS}_{LOF} + \operatorname{SS}_{PE}
}
$$

where:

- $\operatorname{SS}_{PE}$ is pure error
- $\operatorname{SS}_{LOF}$ is the lack-of-fit sum of squares

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{SS}_{LOF}  =  \operatorname{SSE}-\operatorname{SS}_{PE}
}
$$

The lack-of-fit sum of squares measures the additional variation arising
because the fitted straight line does not pass through all the group means.

## Degrees of freedom {style="font-size: 80%;"}

<br>

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column}

### Simple linear regression {.center}

$$
df_{SSE}=n-2
$$

:::

::: {.column}

### Means model {.center}

$$
df_{PE}=n-g
$$

:::
::::

The remaining degrees of freedom are:

$$
df_{LOF} = (n-2)-(n-g) = g-2
$$

The decomposition is therefore:

| Source | Sum of squares | Degrees of freedom |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Lack of fit | $\operatorname{SS}_{LOF}$ | $g-2$ |
| Pure error | $\operatorname{SS}_{PE}$ | $n-g$ |
| Regression residual | $\operatorname{SSE}$ | $n-2$ |

## The lack-of-fit test {style="font-size: 80%;"}

We test whether the straight-line model is adequate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
H_0:\quad &\text{The linear regression model is adequate}\\
H_A:\quad &\text{The linear regression model has lack of fit}
\end{aligned}
$$

The test statistic is:

$$
\boxed{
F= \frac{ \operatorname{SS}_{LOF}/(g-2) }{ \operatorname{SS}_{PE}/(n-g)
}
}
$$

Under $H_0$, assuming the normal linear model conditions,

$$
F\sim F_{g-2,\,n-g}
$$

We reject $H_0$ for large values of $F$

## Interpreting the test

- A **small** $F$-statistic indicates that the lack-of-fit variation is
small relative to the pure error variation.
- A **large** $F$-statistic indicates that the fitted line differs
substantially from the group means, relative to the random variation within groups.

- A small p-value provides evidence that the straight-line model does not adequately
  describe the relationship.
- A large p-value means that we do not have sufficient evidence of lack of fit. It does
  not prove that the model is correct.

## Extending the test to multiple regression {style="font-size: 80%;"}

The same idea extends to multiple regression

Replicates must have the same values for **all predictors**.

If there are $g$ distinct combinations of predictor values and the
full regression model estimates $p$ parameters, then:

$$
df_{LOF}=g-p, \qquad df_{PE}=n-g
$$

The lack-of-fit statistic becomes:

$$
F= \frac{ \{\operatorname{SSE}-\operatorname{SS}_{PE}\}/(g-p) }{ \operatorname{SS}_{PE}/(n-g) }.
$$

The test requires sufficient replication to estimate pure error.

## Let's do an example {style="font-size: 60%;"}

### Voltage data

Batches of electrical fluid were subjected to constant voltages until
their insulating properties broke down.

The variables are:

- $Y$: time until breakdown.
- $X$: applied voltage.

We want to understand how breakdown time changes with voltage.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8a

voltage |>
  ggplot(aes(x = voltage, y = time)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Voltage",
    y = "Time to breakdown"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Fitting a model

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8b
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

fit_1 <- lm(log(time) ~ voltage, data = voltage)

summary(fit_1)
```

## Checking the fitted relationship

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8c

p_1 <- voltage |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(fit_1),
    log_time = log(time)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = voltage, y = log_time)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Voltage",
    y = "Log time to breakdown"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_1
```

## Let's fit a means model

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8d
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true
fit_2 <- lm(log(time) ~ factor(voltage), data = voltage)

summary(fit_2)
```

## Checking the fitted relationship

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8e

p_2 <- voltage |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(fit_2),
    log_time = log(time)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = voltage, y = log_time)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted), linewidth = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Voltage",
    y = "Log time to breakdown"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p_2
```


---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8f

ggpubr::ggarrange(plotlist = c(p_1, p_2))
```

## Comparing both models {style="font-size: 80%;"}

```{r}
#| label: chunk-8g
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

anova(fit_1, fit_2)
```


:::: {.fragment .fade-up}
::: {.callout-important}

## What have we learned from the voltage example?

There are two different questions:

1. Is there evidence of a relationship between voltage and log breakdown
   time?
2. Is a straight-line relationship an adequate description of that
  relationship?

The first question is addressed by testing the regression slope.

The second is addressed by the lack-of-fit test.

A significant regression coefficient does not automatically imply that the
model is adequate.

:::
::::

## Diagnostic plots

```{r}
#| label: chunk-9

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(fit_1, which = 1)
plot(fit_1, which = 2)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

# Added variable plots {background-color="#40666e"}

## Assessing predictors in multiple regression {style="font-size: 70%;"}

In simple linear regression, we can assess the relationship between $Y$
and $X$ using:

- the scatterplot of $Y$ against $X$
- the estimated slope
- the $t$-test for the slope
- the regression sum of squares
- $R^2$.

::: {.callout-important}
## In multiple regression, the situation is more complicated.

A predictor may be related to the response simply because it is related
to another predictor already in the model.

We therefore want to assess the contribution of a predictor
**after accounting for the other predictors**.
:::

## What does an added variable plot show?

<br>

::: {.callout-warning}
## An **added variable plot** displays the relationship between:

- the part of the response not explained by the other predictors;
- the part of the predictor not explained by the other predictors.

It allows us to visualise the adjusted relationship between the response and one predictor.
:::

For example, suppose we want to assess whether `prod` should be added to a
model that already contains `temp` and `inv`.

We need to remove the effects of `temp` and `inv` from both `steam` and `prod`.

## Constructing an added variable plot

To assess `prod` after accounting for `temp` and `inv`, carry out two regressions.

**Step 1: Remove the effects of `temp` and `inv` from the response.**

Fit:

$$
\text{steam}
=
\alpha_0+\alpha_1\text{temp}
+\alpha_2\text{inv}+\text{error}.
$$

Save the residuals:

$$
e(\text{steam}\mid\text{temp},\text{inv}).
$$

These residuals represent the part of `steam` not explained by `temp` and `inv`.

## Constructing an added variable plot

**Step 2: Remove the effects of `temp` and `inv` from `prod`.**

Fit:

$$
\text{prod}
=
\gamma_0+\gamma_1\text{temp}
+\gamma_2\text{inv}+\text{error}.
$$

Save the residuals:

$$
e(\text{prod}\mid\text{temp},\text{inv}).
$$

These residuals represent the part of `prod` not explained by `temp` and `inv`.

**Step 3: Plot the two sets of residuals.**

$$
\boxed{
\text{Plot }
e(\text{steam}\mid\text{temp},\text{inv})
\text{ against }
e(\text{prod}\mid\text{temp},\text{inv})
}
$$

This is the added variable plot for `prod`.

## Interpreting the added variable plot

The plot shows whether the part of `prod` not explained by `temp` and `inv` is associated with the part of `steam` not explained by those same predictors.

- A clear linear pattern suggests that `prod` contributes information beyond `temp` and `inv`.
- Little or no pattern suggests that `prod` may add little explanatory information.
- Unusual points may indicate observations that have substantial influence on the apparent adjusted relationship.

The plot focuses on the contribution of `prod` **after controlling for** the other predictors.

## Added variable plots for the steam data

First, fit the two regressions used to obtain the residuals.

```{r}
#| label: chunk-10a
#| echo: true
fit_steam <- lm(steam ~ temp + inv, data = steam)
fit_prod <- lm(prod ~ temp + inv, data = steam)

steam_resid <- resid(fit_steam)
prod_resid <- resid(fit_prod)
```

---

<br>

```{r}
#| label: chunk-10b
tibble(
  prod_resid = prod_resid,
  steam_resid = steam_resid
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = prod_resid, y = steam_resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "prod residuals after temp and inv",
    y = "steam residuals after temp and inv",
    title = "Added variable plot for prod"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Partial $R^2$ {style="font-size: 60%;"}

The partial $R^2$ for `prod`, given `temp` and `inv`, measures the
proportion of the variation remaining after fitting `temp` and `inv`
that is explained by adding `prod`.

$$
R^2_{\; \text{PROD}\mid\text{TEMP, INV}} = \frac{ \operatorname{SSR}(B\mid A) }{ \operatorname{SSE}(A)
},
$$

where:

- Model A contains `TEMP` and `INV`.
- Model B contains `TEMP`, `INV` and `PROD`.


::: {.fragment .fade-up}

$$
R^2_{\text{PROD}\mid\text{TEMP, INV}} =
\frac{0.004}{8.931} \approx 0.00045.
$$

This is approximately $0.045\%$.

Therefore, `prod` explains very little of the variation remaining after
`temp` and `inv` have been included.

:::

---

<br>


::: {.callout}

## Key messages

- A smaller SSE does not automatically justify a larger model.
- Sequential sums of squares depend on the order in which predictors are entered.
- A significant regression relationship does not guarantee that the chosen
  model fits adequately.
- Added variable plots help us understand the unique contribution of individual
  predictors.

The central idea is to assess not only how well a model fits the observed
data, but also whether its structure is appropriate and whether each predictor
contributes useful information.

:::
